_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 1 Follow, Edit, Correct. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order (linear; following; understanding; correcting; editing), then the lesson's own four-verb sorter. Every wrong algorithm is drawn by handing the LESSON'S OWN scene the wrong list - ART.scene(smoothie, [banana, berries, milk, pour]) and ART.scene(smoothie, [banana, berries, milk, blend]) - so the kit paints the lumps and the splat and writes its own caption, and the film draws no picture of a mistake.
title: Follow, Edit, Correct
subtitle: Grade 3 Computing
objectives: Follow, understand, edit and correct linear algorithms.
Know that logical thinking is used in the creation of algorithms.

beats.say: Six steps, in a line: banana, strawberries, milk, lid, blend, pour.
Follow it. Understand it. Edit it. Correct it. Four things, one algorithm.
A linear algorithm is a line of steps: a first, a next, a next, and an end.
Making a smoothie is linear. Banana first, then strawberries, then milk.
Then the lid on, then blend, then pour. Six steps, one after another.
You go top to bottom. You never jump back up the list.
Linear does not mean short. It means in order, one after another, and it can be long.
Following an algorithm means doing the step it names next.
And only that step. The algorithm says lid, so you put the lid on.
Not blend, even if you would like to. Blend comes after the lid.
A computer does exactly this. A wrong step makes a wrong thing happen.
Understanding is not the same as following. It means knowing why.
Why does the lid go on before you blend it?

at.lid: the lid go on before you blend it

beats.say: Take the lid step out and blend anyway. Smoothie round the kitchen!
Pour last, because you pour what the blender has made smooth.
Every step is where it is for a reason. That reasoning is logical thinking.
Sometimes a step is wrong. Correcting means putting the right step in its place.
This kite algorithm says: cross the sticks, tie them, cut the paper into tiny pieces.

at.tiny: cut the paper into tiny pieces

beats.say: Tiny pieces? The paper has to cover the sticks. That step is the bug.
Take it out and put the right step in. Glue paper over the sticks.
Now run the algorithm again and check. The kite flies!
Editing is not correcting. Nothing is wrong: you want something different.
This tower algorithm is big brick, middle brick, small brick, flag.
You want a red top. Change the small brick step to a red brick.
One step changed, and the tower is different. A red brick on top!
Edit is a change you want. Correct is a fix you need.
There are four things you can do with one algorithm.
Follow: do the steps. Understand: know why each step is there.
Edit: change it because you want to. Correct: fix a step that is wrong.

at.correct: Correct: fix a step that is wrong

beats.say: Swapping jam for honey because you like honey is editing, not correcting.
A linear algorithm is a line of steps, from top to bottom.
You follow it exactly, and you understand why each step is there.
You edit it when you want a change, and correct it when a step is wrong.
